focus: The small-team model: who can talk to, approve for and change a bot, whether memory is shared or per-person, and the smallest sign-in and roles model that works for a few people on one machine or a shared host.
noveltyJustification: 12 of 18 findings are new external evidence from OpenBot's role and sign-in model plus the runtime's state root; 6 are new design inferences that reduce it to three decisions.
keyQuestions: Who can talk to, approve for and change a bot; is memory shared or per-person; what is the smallest sign-in and roles model that works for a few people on one machine or a shared host?
answeredQuestions: Who can talk to, approve for and change a bot; is memory shared or per-person; what is the smallest sign-in and roles model that works for a few people on one machine or a shared host?

label: OpenBot's role model has three values, owner | admin | member: an owner or an admin governs the organization's people, sign-in and policy, a member uses it, and the owner is whoever created the organization while default has admins and no owner.
The role answer is extensible and a client reads a role it does not know as a member.
A self-hosted install puts everybody who signs in into one shared organization, default.
An organization the caller is not in answers exactly as one that does not exist, default included.
A single-person install has no sign-in at all: it signs nobody in, so it has neither OAuth nor API keys, and key and session operations answer 503 SIGN_IN_UNAVAILABLE.
A single-person install has no OAuth because there is nobody to authorize an app as.
API keys act as the person who made them, start obk_, and only a person signed in to the web app can make or delete one.
There is an openbot-cli OAuth public client beside the desktop and mobile ones, using PKCE S256 with a loopback redirect only.
Skilled has no sign-in, no roles and no organization: state is keyed by repository identity owner/name and the only identity dimension is the checkout.
The state root is per-OS-user by default ($HOME/.local/state), so on a shared host each person gets their own state root and therefore their own memory and needs-you items.
Every state folder is created mode 0o700, so a state root shared between two people would be unreadable by the second one.
bots answer has no role check, so whoever can run the CLI can approve.
The smallest model is OpenBot's single-person install: no sign-in, no OAuth, no API keys, and the OS user is the identity.

Two roles suffice, not three: owner for whoever installed the jobs and member for everyone else, because admin exists to govern people, sign-in and policy and a machine with no sign-in has none of those.
The role should be a file, not a session: one operators.json under the state root listing who may approve, read by bots answer before it writes.
Shared versus per-person memory is a state-root choice, not a code change: a per-user root gives per-person memory and a shared root gives shared memory.
The one change a shared host needs is the folder mode: 0o700 becomes 0o770 with a group so a second person can read the shared root.
The smallest sign-in and roles model for a few people is three decisions and no new service: no sign-in, two roles in one file, and a state root that is either per-user or shared by group.

reason: OpenBot's own single-person install has none, and a few people on one machine already have an OS identity a session would only duplicate.
admin governs people, sign-in and policy; with no sign-in there is nothing for it to govern, so it collapses into owner.
The state root's owner and mode already decide who can read and write, and a token would be a second authority that can disagree with the filesystem.
OpenBot scopes memory to the person and the organization, and a per-bot store would make a person's facts disappear when the bot is renamed.
